name: Ngorongoro Conservation Area
subtitle: A mixed property on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1979, where wildlife and Maasai herders share the same land.

facts.label: Established
facts.value: 1959, as a multiple land use area

facts.label: Maasai at inscription
facts.value: An estimated 20,000 people, with some 275,000 head of livestock

parts.text: UNESCO describes the property in these words: “The Ngorongoro Conservation Area spans vast expanses of highland plains, savanna, savanna woodlands and forests. Established in 1959 as a multiple land use area, with wildlife coexisting with semi-nomadic Maasai pastoralists practicing traditional livestock grazing, it includes the spectacular Ngorongoro Crater, the world’s largest caldera.”

sections.title: Herders and wildlife on the same land

parts.text: UNESCO's record says the property “provides grazing land for semi-nomadic Maasai pastoralists”, and that at the time of inscription “an estimated 20,000 Maasai were living in the property, with some 275,000 head of livestock”.

The same record names the tension: it lists “increasing sedentarisation, local overgrazing and agricultural encroachment” as threats, and says one of the management goals is to “protect the interests of the Maasai pastoralists”.

The area also holds a long record of human evolution. UNESCO cites “fossilized footprints at Laetoli, associated with the development of human bipedalism” and the sequence of hominin species found in Olduvai Gorge.

gaps: Independent sources. Every fact here comes from UNESCO's own record, so it is one voice, written by the institution that manages the listing.

How the area is governed today, including any moves of residents out of it, is not covered here: the UNESCO record reflects the inscription and its periodic reviews. Reporting and research on this should be cited before the card is published.
Maasai voices: none yet. The record describes the Maasai from outside.
